concepts.name: Grounds for Proclamation of National Emergency
key_dimensions: Three grounds: war, external aggression, armed rebellion (NOT internal disturbance — changed by 44th Amendment)
Original Constitution used 'internal disturbance'; 44th Amendment 1978 substituted 'armed rebellion' — a UPSC trap
Distinction between 'external aggression' vs 'war' — Emergency can be proclaimed even before actual war begins
Imminent danger clause: Emergency can be proclaimed on grounds of imminent threat, not just actual occurrence

concepts.name: Cabinet's Written Recommendation — Pre-condition for Proclamation
key_dimensions: 44th Amendment made it mandatory that Union Cabinet (not just PM) must send written recommendation to President
President cannot proclaim National Emergency on his own or on PM's verbal advice alone
This was a direct response to 1975 Emergency proclaimed on PM Indira Gandhi's advice alone
Distinguishes National Emergency from President's Rule (Article 356) where Cabinet recommendation is not mandatory in writing

concepts.name: Parliamentary Approval: Procedure and Time Limits
key_dimensions: Must be approved by both Houses within ONE month of proclamation (44th Amendment reduced it from 2 months)
Approval requires Special Majority: majority of total membership AND 2/3rd majority of members present and voting
If Lok Sabha is dissolved before approval, proclamation survives for 30 days after reconstitution of Lok Sabha, provided Rajya Sabha has approved it
Contrast with President's Rule (Article 356) approval timeline of 2 months — a frequent UPSC trap

concepts.name: Special Majority Requirement and its Uniqueness
key_dimensions: Requires majority of total membership of each House (absolute majority) PLUS 2/3rd of members present and voting
This double-condition special majority is unique to Emergency provisions — different from Constitutional Amendment majority under Article 368
Both Houses must separately pass — joint sitting is NOT applicable for Emergency approval
Contrasting trap: Ordinary legislation requires simple majority; Constitutional amendments require special majority under Article 368

concepts.name: Duration and Continuation of National Emergency
key_dimensions: Once approved, operates for 6 months and can be extended indefinitely by 6-month intervals with fresh parliamentary approval each time
Each extension also requires the same special majority in both Houses
No maximum limit on total duration — can theoretically last indefinitely with periodic renewals
Contrast: President's Rule has a maximum cap of 3 years total (with specific conditions after 1 year)

concepts.name: Revocation of National Emergency
key_dimensions: President can revoke at any time without parliamentary approval — revocation does NOT require special majority
44th Amendment introduced: President MUST revoke if Lok Sabha passes a simple majority resolution disapproving continuance
Special sitting of Lok Sabha: if 1/10th of total Lok Sabha members give written notice, Speaker must convene special sitting within 14 days
Rajya Sabha has NO role in revocation — only Lok Sabha can force revocation, making this a Lok Sabha-exclusive power

concepts.name: Effect on Fundamental Rights — Articles 358 and 359
key_dimensions: Article 358: Automatic suspension of Article 19 (six freedoms) ONLY during war or external aggression — NOT during armed rebellion
Article 359: President can suspend the RIGHT TO MOVE courts for enforcement of Fundamental Rights (except Articles 20 and 21)
Articles 20 and 21 can NEVER be suspended even during National Emergency — 44th Amendment guarantee
Key trap: Article 358 is automatic; Article 359 requires a separate Presidential Order — two different mechanisms

concepts.name: Effect on Centre-State Relations During National Emergency
key_dimensions: Parliament becomes empowered to legislate on State List subjects (Article 250) — though State Legislature is not suspended
Executive power of Union extends to giving directions to states on ANY matter (Article 353)
Centre can modify constitutional provisions regarding distribution of revenues between Centre and states (Article 354)
State Legislatures continue to function but their laws can be overridden by Parliament — federal character suspended, not abolished

concepts.name: Effect on Lok Sabha's Term During National Emergency
key_dimensions: Parliament can extend Lok Sabha's term by one year at a time (by law) for the duration of Emergency
Extension cannot continue beyond 6 months after Emergency ceases — Lok Sabha must be dissolved within that period
This was used during 1962 and 1971 emergencies to extend Lok Sabha terms
Rajya Sabha term is NOT affected — being a permanent house, it cannot be dissolved or extended

concepts.name: Judicial Review of National Emergency — Minerva Mills and Related Cases
key_dimensions: Originally, 38th Amendment (1975) made Presidential satisfaction non-justiciable — courts could not review
44th Amendment removed this immunity; Supreme Court can review if proclamation is based on irrelevant/mala fide grounds
Minerva Mills (1980): SC reaffirmed limited judicial review; judicial review itself is part of Basic Structure
State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977): Court held proclamation under Article 356 (analogous reasoning) has limited but real judicial scrutiny

concepts.name: Scope of Article 352: 'Part of Territory' vs. Whole Country
key_dimensions: 44th Amendment: National Emergency can be proclaimed for the whole of India OR a part of its territory
Allows targeted/limited emergency — a significant change from original Constitution which covered whole country
This prevents misuse of blanket emergency when threat is localized to a border region
Contrasting trap: President's Rule (Article 356) applies to a specific state — not the whole country

concepts.name: National Emergency vs. President's Rule vs. Financial Emergency — Comparative Framework
key_dimensions: Article 352 (National Emergency), Article 356 (State Emergency/President's Rule), Article 360 (Financial Emergency) — three distinct types
Grounds, approval process, duration, and effects on federalism differ significantly across all three
National Emergency affects fundamental rights; Financial Emergency affects salary/allowance provisions; President's Rule affects state executive/legislature
Simultaneous operation: All three can co-exist — Constitution does not bar concurrent proclamations

concepts.name: Proclamations of National Emergency in India — Historical Instances
key_dimensions: Three proclamations: 1962 (China war — external aggression), 1971 (Pakistan war — external aggression), 1975 (internal disturbance — controversial)
1962 and 1971 Emergencies: Proclaimed on ground of external aggression — justified and largely uncontested
1975 Emergency: Proclaimed on 'internal disturbance' ground — led to 44th Amendment replacing it with 'armed rebellion'
1962 Emergency was revoked in 1968; 1971 Emergency co-existed with 1962 Emergency — two simultaneous emergencies

concepts.name: Role of Rajya Sabha in National Emergency — Powers and Limitations
key_dimensions: Rajya Sabha must also approve proclamation with special majority — it is NOT a subordinate house here
However, Rajya Sabha has NO role in revocation — Lok Sabha alone can pass disapproval resolution
If Lok Sabha is dissolved at time of proclamation, Rajya Sabha alone can approve (temporary approval), but Lok Sabha must ratify within 30 days of reconstitution
This asymmetry (equal in approval, absent in revocation) is a classic UPSC trap question

concepts.name: Impact on Legislative Powers of Parliament During Emergency
key_dimensions: Parliament acquires power to legislate on State List subjects under Article 250 — concurrent power, not exclusive
State laws on State List subjects do not become void — they remain operative; Parliamentary law prevails to extent of inconsistency
Laws made by Parliament under emergency powers lapse within 6 months of revocation (Article 250(2))
Distinction: Under Article 249 (National interest), Parliamentary laws on State List also lapse 6 months after resolution — similar but different trigger

concepts.name: Article 19 Suspension — Scope and Limitations (Article 358)
key_dimensions: Article 358 suspends Article 19 automatically ONLY when Emergency is declared on grounds of war or external aggression — NOT armed rebellion
44th Amendment introduced this restriction — originally Article 19 was suspended for all types of National Emergency
Suspension means State can make laws and take executive actions inconsistent with Article 19 without challenge
However, laws made under Article 358 must have 'reasonable nexus' with the Emergency — cannot use it to pass unrelated laws

concepts.name: President's Satisfaction and the 'Imminent Danger' Clause
key_dimensions: Article 352 allows proclamation even before actual war/aggression if President is satisfied that there is 'imminent danger'
Imminent danger of war is different from imminent danger of internal disturbance — only the former triggers Emergency
Presidential satisfaction is now subject to limited judicial review post-44th Amendment
The phrase 'is satisfied' indicates subjective satisfaction, but courts can check if it is based on relevant material

concepts.name: Effect of National Emergency on Financial Provisions — Article 354
key_dimensions: During National Emergency, Parliament can modify provisions related to distribution of taxes between Centre and States (Article 270)
This modification must be laid before Parliament and ceases to operate at the end of the financial year in which Emergency ends
Distinct from Financial Emergency (Article 360) — Article 354 operates within National Emergency framework
States lose financial autonomy but Centre cannot permanently alter the Finance Commission's recommendations

concepts.name: 44th Amendment Act 1978 — Comprehensive Safeguards Against Misuse
key_dimensions: 'Internal disturbance' replaced by 'armed rebellion' — raising the threshold for proclamation
Cabinet's written recommendation made mandatory before Presidential proclamation
Parliamentary approval period reduced from 2 months to 1 month; special majority requirement added
Articles 20 and 21 made non-suspendable; Lok Sabha given power to revoke by simple majority; judicial review restored — all in one amendment

concepts.name: Relationship Between National Emergency and Federalism
key_dimensions: India becomes 'more unitary' but NOT a unitary state — states continue to exist, legislatures continue to function
Dr. Ambedkar's phrase: Constitution becomes 'unitary in spirit, federal in form' during Emergency
State Legislative Assemblies are not dissolved or suspended — they lose concurrent legislative power to Parliament
Post-Emergency, Centre-state relationship reverts automatically — no formal restoration needed, unlike President's Rule restoration
